title: Asthma Diagnosis and Stepwise Management
bottomLine: Asthma requires a compatible variable symptom pattern plus objective evidence of variable expiratory airflow limitation whenever feasible. Do not treat chronic symptoms indefinitely without confirming the diagnosis, and do not rely on short-acting bronchodilator rescue alone when controller therapy is indicated.
recognize: Episodic wheeze, cough, chest tightness and dyspnea that vary over time or with triggers support asthma.
Night symptoms, exercise limitation, recurrent steroid bursts or urgent visits suggest poor control and higher future risk.
Normal spirometry between episodes does not exclude asthma; repeat testing or alternative objective confirmation may be needed.
differentiate: COPD, inducible laryngeal obstruction, heart failure, bronchiectasis, reflux, chronic rhinosinusitis and dysfunctional breathing can mimic asthma.
Acute severe asthma is a physiologic emergency and should not be managed as routine step-up therapy.
assessment: Assess symptom frequency, nighttime waking, activity limitation, reliever use, exacerbation history, smoking/vaping, occupational exposures, pregnancy, adherence and inhaler technique.
Look for hypoxemia, inability to speak, fatigue, altered consciousness or a silent chest during an exacerbation.
workup: Use spirometry with bronchodilator response when available; use serial peak-flow or other objective approaches when spirometry is nondiagnostic but suspicion remains.
Investigate alternative diagnoses or comorbidities when symptoms persist despite apparently adequate therapy.
management: Use an inhaled-corticosteroid-containing controller strategy matched to symptom burden and exacerbation risk, then step treatment up or down only after reassessing diagnosis, adherence, technique and exposures.
Provide a written asthma action plan and manage rhinitis, smoking/vaping and other modifiable contributors.
Severe or refractory asthma warrants specialist assessment rather than indefinite empiric escalation.
medicationSafety: Repeated systemic corticosteroid bursts carry cumulative harm; poor control should trigger controller optimization and diagnosis review.
Teach inhaler-specific technique and mouth rinsing where appropriate; check interactions and pregnancy context before medication changes.
redFlags: Silent chest or minimal air movement
Markedly reduced peak flow with severe symptoms
Failure to respond to initial bronchodilator therapy
counselling: Teach trigger reduction, controller adherence, inhaler technique, action-plan zones and when to seek emergency care.
Explain that feeling well between attacks does not mean airway inflammation/risk is absent.
followUp: Reassess control, exacerbations, technique and adherence after treatment changes and periodically thereafter.
Consider specialist referral for diagnostic uncertainty, frequent exacerbations or need for high-intensity therapy.
examTrap: Escalating medications for months without confirming variable airflow obstruction or checking inhaler technique and adherence.
oneLinePearl: Confirm variable airflow limitation, then treat both today’s symptoms and tomorrow’s exacerbation risk.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society current asthma guidance and guideline library
Canadian respiratory practice standards

title: COPD Diagnosis, Severity, and Management
bottomLine: COPD is confirmed with persistent post-bronchodilator airflow obstruction in the right clinical context. Management is driven by symptoms, exacerbations, smoking/exposure risk and comorbidity—not spirometry alone.
recognize: Progressive exertional dyspnea, chronic cough/sputum and exposure history raise suspicion.
Frequent exacerbations, weight loss, hypoxemia, hypercapnia or declining function signal higher risk.
Consider alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency when disease is early, disproportionate or otherwise suggestive.
differentiate: Asthma has greater variability/reversibility; heart failure, ILD, bronchiectasis and deconditioning can mimic or coexist with COPD.
An exacerbation requires exclusion of pneumonia, PE, pneumothorax and heart failure when the presentation is atypical or severe.
assessment: Assess smoking/vaping and occupational exposure, symptom burden, exacerbation history, inhaler use, exercise tolerance, weight, oxygenation, vaccination and comorbid cardiovascular disease.
During acute worsening assess work of breathing, oxygenation, mental status and signs of pneumonia/PE/heart failure.
workup: Confirm chronic COPD with spirometry; use chest imaging, CBC, ECG, BNP, D-dimer/CT or other testing only when the differential warrants it.
Assess resting/exertional oxygenation when clinically indicated and evaluate hypercapnia when severe disease or ventilatory failure is possible.
management: Smoking cessation, vaccination, exercise/pulmonary rehabilitation and inhaled bronchodilator therapy are foundational.

Use long-acting bronchodilator combinations and inhaled corticosteroid-containing therapy selectively according to exacerbation history and eosinophilic/asthma features rather than automatically for every patient.
Exacerbations require prompt bronchodilation, targeted systemic corticosteroid/antibiotic use when indicated, and escalation for respiratory failure.
medicationSafety: Inhaled corticosteroids can increase pneumonia risk in selected COPD patients and should have a clear indication.
Review anticholinergic, beta-agonist and systemic steroid adverse effects and ensure device technique matches patient ability.
counselling: Teach inhaler technique, exacerbation action planning, smoking cessation and pulmonary rehabilitation benefits.
Discuss goals of care early in advanced disease rather than only during crisis.
followUp: Track symptoms, exacerbations, adherence, technique and functional status; repeat spirometry when it will change management.
Refer for advanced therapies or diagnostic uncertainty when appropriate.
examTrap: Diagnosing COPD from smoking history and symptoms without spirometric confirmation—or prescribing inhaled corticosteroid to everyone with COPD.
oneLinePearl: COPD diagnosis is spirometric; treatment intensity is clinical.
sourceBasis: 2023 Canadian Thoracic Society Guideline on Pharmacotherapy in Stable COPD
Canadian Thoracic Society 2025 alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency guideline

title: Pneumonia: Community vs Hospital Acquired
bottomLine: Pneumonia is a clinical-radiographic syndrome, not crackles plus antibiotics. Determine setting, severity, host risk and likely resistance before selecting therapy; hospital-acquired disease requires a different pathogen and resistance framework than uncomplicated community-acquired pneumonia.
recognize: Fever, cough, dyspnea, pleuritic pain, hypoxemia or focal chest findings can support pneumonia, but presentations in older adults may be subtle.
Recent hospitalization, ventilation, antibiotics, structural lung disease and immune compromise alter pathogen/resistance risk.
differentiate: Acute bronchitis and viral URI usually lack focal consolidation; heart failure, PE and aspiration pneumonitis can mimic pneumonia.
Aspiration pneumonitis after a witnessed event may improve without antibiotics unless secondary bacterial infection develops.
assessment: Assess respiratory rate, oxygenation, blood pressure, mental status, oral intake, comorbidity, immune status and recent healthcare/antibiotic exposure.
Use severity and social context to decide outpatient versus hospital care.
workup: When pneumonia is suspected and access is reasonable, obtain chest imaging to confirm new infiltrate/consolidation rather than prescribing from crackles alone.
Cultures and broader diagnostics are selected by severity, treatment failure, immune status and resistant-organism risk.
management: Use current Canadian/local antimicrobial guidance matched to community versus hospital acquisition, allergy, renal function and resistance risk.
Use the shortest evidence-supported effective duration and reassess diagnosis/response rather than automatically extending antibiotics.
Escalate hypoxemic, septic or otherwise unstable patients and address source-control/complications such as empyema.
medicationSafety: Avoid unnecessary broad-spectrum therapy because of C. difficile, drug toxicity and resistance.
Adjust renally cleared antibiotics and review QT/drug interactions when relevant.
counselling: Give explicit return precautions for worsening dyspnea, fever, confusion, dehydration or chest pain.
Explain why antibiotics are not useful when objective evidence supports a viral/nonbacterial syndrome.
followUp: Reassess clinical response and microbiology; reconsider the diagnosis when improvement is absent.
Arrange follow-up imaging selectively when age/risk/persistent symptoms make an obstructing lesion or malignancy plausible.
examTrap: Prescribing antibiotics for suspected pneumonia from crackles alone in a stable patient without objective evidence when chest imaging is readily available.
oneLinePearl: Pneumonia treatment starts by confirming the syndrome and defining the setting.
sourceBasis: Choosing Wisely Canada Using Antibiotics Wisely — pneumonia guidance
Canadian antimicrobial stewardship principles

title: Pulmonary Nodule Evaluation and Follow-Up
bottomLine: A pulmonary nodule is a risk-stratification problem. Compare prior imaging, define size/morphology and patient cancer risk, then use the appropriate surveillance or diagnostic pathway; not every nodule needs biopsy and not every small nodule is benign.
recognize: Risk rises with age, smoking history, growth, spiculation, upper-lobe location and suspicious morphology.
Stability over appropriate time lowers concern, but required surveillance varies with nodule type.
differentiate: Screen-detected nodules are managed within a screening program/risk framework; incidental nodules use incidental-nodule pathways.
Infection/inflammation, granuloma and metastasis are alternatives to primary lung cancer.
assessment: Review smoking/exposure history, prior malignancy, family history, symptoms, immune status and all prior chest imaging.
Ask about hemoptysis, weight loss, persistent cough and other findings that convert a screening/incidental issue into diagnostic evaluation.
workup: Characterize nodule size, density and morphology and compare with prior imaging.
Use interval CT, PET/CT, bronchoscopy or tissue sampling according to malignancy probability and local specialist pathway rather than reflex biopsy.
management: Use a documented surveillance plan with the next study/date/owner.
Refer suspicious, enlarging or higher-risk lesions to respirology/thoracic oncology.
Manage infection/inflammatory differentials when the imaging/clinical pattern supports them.
medicationSafety: Avoid empiric repeated antibiotic courses for an unresolved nodule without evidence of infection.
Consider anticoagulation/bleeding risk before biopsy planning.
counselling: Explain that surveillance is an active safety plan, not 'doing nothing'.
Use non-stigmatizing smoking cessation support and discuss radiation/false-positive tradeoffs when relevant.
followUp: Close the loop on every recommended CT or referral; incidental nodules are a common source of lost follow-up.
examTrap: Biopsying every small incidental nodule—or failing to compare prior imaging before creating a new surveillance plan.
oneLinePearl: Nodule care is risk plus growth plus ownership of follow-up.
sourceBasis: Canadian lung-cancer screening and thoracic imaging practice principles
Provincial lung diagnostic pathways

title: Interstitial Lung Disease Recognition and Referral
bottomLine: Progressive exertional dyspnea with dry cough, inspiratory crackles, diffusion impairment or fibrotic imaging should trigger an ILD pathway rather than repeated treatment for asthma or infection. Define exposures, autoimmune clues and severity early and refer suspected fibrotic ILD appropriately.
recognize: Dry cough, progressive exertional dyspnea and bibasal inspiratory crackles are common clues.
Autoimmune disease, medications, occupational/environmental exposures and hypersensitivity can produce ILD.
Acute worsening can represent infection, PE, heart failure or an acute ILD exacerbation.
differentiate: COPD/asthma are obstructive syndromes; ILD commonly causes restriction and reduced diffusion but PFT patterns are not diagnostic alone.
Heart failure and infection can produce interstitial imaging abnormalities and must be distinguished clinically.
assessment: Take detailed occupational, environmental, bird/mould, medication, smoking and connective-tissue-disease histories.
Assess oxygenation at rest/exertion, functional decline and systemic autoimmune findings.
workup: Obtain chest imaging with high-resolution CT when ILD is suspected, complete PFTs including diffusion capacity, and targeted autoimmune/exposure testing.
Avoid broad empiric immunosuppression before diagnosis and infection-risk assessment.
management: Refer suspected fibrotic ILD to respirology/ILD expertise for multidisciplinary diagnosis and disease-specific treatment.
Address oxygen/exercise/rehabilitation, vaccination, smoking/exposure cessation and comorbidity.
Before immunosuppression, follow current Canadian infection-screening guidance.
medicationSafety: Immunosuppressants and antifibrotic agents require disease-specific indications, interaction review and organ-function monitoring.
Screen for relevant latent/chronic infections before immunosuppression according to current CTS guidance.
counselling: Explain that ILD is a family of disorders and diagnosis often requires integrating HRCT, exposure/autoimmune history and multidisciplinary review.
Discuss pulmonary rehabilitation, oxygen safety and vaccination when indicated.
followUp: Track symptoms, oxygenation, PFTs and imaging at disease-appropriate intervals.
Escalate accelerating decline rather than waiting for routine follow-up.
examTrap: Giving repeated antibiotics or inhalers for progressive restrictive symptoms without obtaining HRCT/PFT-based ILD evaluation.
oneLinePearl: Progressive dyspnea plus crackles and fibrosis belongs on an ILD pathway early.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society fibrotic ILD evaluation/monitoring standards
2026 CTS infection screening before immunosuppression in ILD statement

title: Pulmonary Embolism Risk Stratification and Treatment
bottomLine: PE workup starts with hemodynamic stability and pretest probability. Use D-dimer only when it can safely reduce imaging; a positive D-dimer does not diagnose PE, and an unstable patient needs an emergency imaging/treatment pathway rather than outpatient probability tools.
recognize: Unexplained dyspnea, pleuritic pain, tachycardia, hypoxemia, syncope or hemoptysis can occur.
Cancer, prior VTE, estrogen/pregnancy/postpartum, immobilization and recent surgery increase risk.
differentiate: ACS, pneumonia, pneumothorax, asthma/COPD and heart failure can mimic PE.
Massive/high-risk PE is defined by hemodynamic compromise, not clot size alone.
assessment: Assess BP/perfusion, oxygenation, chest pain, syncope, bleeding risk, pregnancy, renal function and anticoagulant exposure.
Estimate clinical pretest probability before ordering D-dimer or imaging in a stable patient.
workup: Use validated probability/D-dimer pathways and CT pulmonary angiography or V/Q imaging as appropriate.
Use ECG/troponin/BNP/echo findings for severity/right-heart strain, not as standalone diagnostic tests.
management: Start anticoagulation when PE is confirmed or sufficiently likely and bleeding risk permits, using current Thrombosis Canada/local guidance.
Hemodynamically unstable PE requires urgent specialist/acute-care consideration of reperfusion strategies.
Select outpatient treatment only for appropriately risk-stratified stable patients with reliable follow-up.
medicationSafety: Renal function, pregnancy, cancer, body weight, interactions and bleeding risk affect anticoagulant selection.
Do not use INR to measure DOAC effect; follow drug-specific laboratory/clinical monitoring principles.
counselling: Teach bleeding precautions, adherence, interaction review and when recurrent chest pain/dyspnea requires emergency care.
followUp: Reassess anticoagulation duration based on provoking factors, recurrence risk and bleeding risk.
Evaluate persistent dyspnea for chronic thromboembolic disease when indicated.
examTrap: Ordering a D-dimer in a high-probability unstable patient—or treating a positive D-dimer as proof of PE.
oneLinePearl: Probability chooses the test; hemodynamics choose the urgency.
sourceBasis: Thrombosis Canada Pulmonary Embolism clinical guide
Canadian acute-care thrombosis practice

title: Obstructive Sleep Apnea Diagnosis and CPAP Management
bottomLine: OSA is confirmed with sleep testing in the appropriate clinical context; screening questionnaires estimate risk but do not diagnose disease. Treatment decisions integrate symptoms, oxygenation/respiratory burden, comorbidity, anatomy and patient preference—not AHI alone.
recognize: Loud snoring, witnessed apneas, choking/gasping, nonrestorative sleep and daytime sleepiness raise suspicion.
Hypertension, atrial fibrillation, obesity and resistant hypertension increase pretest probability.
Driving/work safety becomes urgent with dangerous sleepiness.
differentiate: Insomnia, restless legs, circadian disorder, medication/substance effects and central sleep apnea can mimic or coexist.
A low-risk questionnaire does not exclude OSA when clinical suspicion remains high.
assessment: Assess snoring/apneas, sleepiness, sleep schedule, driving incidents, sedatives/alcohol, nasal obstruction, cardiometabolic disease and occupation.
Evaluate for hypoventilation/central apnea or cardiopulmonary disease when home testing may be inadequate.
workup: Use home sleep apnea testing or polysomnography according to pretest probability, comorbidity and local sleep-medicine pathway.
Do not diagnose OSA from symptoms/questionnaire alone.
management: CPAP is first-line for many symptomatic/moderate-severe patients; alternatives include weight-focused care, mandibular advancement devices, positional/anatomic strategies and specialty management when appropriate.
Treat nasal obstruction and modifiable sedative/alcohol contributors.
Address driving restrictions when sleepiness creates risk according to provincial/territorial rules.
medicationSafety: Sedatives, opioids and alcohol can worsen sleep-disordered breathing and daytime impairment.
CPAP adherence problems should prompt mask/pressure/comfort troubleshooting rather than declaring treatment failure immediately.
counselling: Teach CPAP setup, humidification, mask care and why adherence matters.
Discuss sleep hygiene and weight management without implying OSA is solely weight-caused.
followUp: Review adherence/device data, residual symptoms and mask leak; reassess diagnosis or alternate disorders when symptoms persist despite effective CPAP.
examTrap: Diagnosing OSA from a STOP-BANG score alone or ignoring dangerous driving sleepiness because the formal sleep study is months away.
oneLinePearl: Screening estimates risk; sleep testing confirms OSA; symptoms and risk determine treatment urgency.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society / Canadian Sleep Society sleep-disordered breathing guidance
Canadian sleep medicine practice standards

title: Pleural Effusion Differential Diagnosis and Workup
bottomLine: A new unilateral or unexplained pleural effusion requires cause-directed evaluation. Separate likely transudative systemic disease from exudative infection, malignancy, inflammatory disease and PE, and drain urgently when physiology or infection demands it.
recognize: Dyspnea, pleuritic pain and decreased breath sounds/dullness may occur, but small effusions can be incidental.
Bilateral effusions with clear decompensated heart failure context differ from a new unilateral exudative-appearing effusion.
differentiate: Heart failure/cirrhosis/nephrotic states commonly produce transudative physiology; pneumonia, malignancy, TB, PE and autoimmune disease are important exudative causes.
Empyema is infected pleural space and requires drainage/source control, not antibiotics alone.
assessment: Assess oxygenation, fever, pleuritic pain, malignancy risk, heart/renal/liver failure, PE risk, TB exposure and immune status.
Look for hemodynamic/respiratory compromise and loculation/complex infection clues.
workup: Use chest imaging and ultrasound; diagnostic thoracentesis is appropriate for many new unexplained or nonclassic effusions.
Pleural studies are chosen to classify cause and infection/malignancy risk; avoid tapping an obvious small stable bilateral heart-failure effusion without a clinical question.
management: Treat the underlying cause.
Drain complicated parapneumonic effusion/empyema and urgently manage large effusions causing significant respiratory compromise.
Refer persistent/recurrent unexplained effusions for pleural specialist evaluation.
medicationSafety: Review anticoagulants/antiplatelets and bleeding risk before thoracentesis according to procedure guidance.
Avoid repeated diuresis for a unilateral exudative pattern without diagnostic reconsideration.
counselling: Explain why fluid sampling is sometimes diagnostic rather than simply therapeutic.
Provide return precautions for worsening breathlessness, fever or chest pain.
followUp: Close the loop on cytology/culture and interval imaging.
Recurrent malignant/chylous/unexplained effusions require specialty planning.
examTrap: Assuming every pleural effusion in a patient with heart disease is heart failure without considering unilateral, febrile or malignant features.
oneLinePearl: New unexplained pleural fluid deserves a cause, not just a diuretic.
sourceBasis: Canadian respiratory/pleural-procedure practice standards
Canadian Thoracic Society chest procedure resources

title: Hemoptysis Evaluation and Management
bottomLine: Hemoptysis is triaged by airway/hemodynamic threat and cause, not by an imprecise volume estimate alone. Confirm the blood is pulmonary, identify cancer/infection/PE/bronchiectasis risks, and escalate immediately when bleeding threatens ventilation or perfusion.
recognize: Blood-streaked sputum may occur with infection or airway disease; brisk/recurrent bleeding raises malignancy, bronchiectasis, TB, vascular and anticoagulation concerns.
Life-threatening hemoptysis is defined by physiologic threat—airway obstruction, hypoxemia or instability—not a universal millilitre cutoff.
differentiate: Epistaxis/oropharyngeal bleeding and hematemesis can mimic hemoptysis.
PE, TB and lung cancer may present with hemoptysis even when chest findings are subtle.
assessment: Assess airway, oxygenation, hemodynamics, bleeding rate, anticoagulants, smoking/cancer risk, TB exposure, infection symptoms and VTE risk.
Look for anemia, coagulopathy, unilateral findings and systemic illness.
workup: Use chest radiograph initially in many stable patients, then CT/CT angiography and bronchoscopy according to severity and suspected source.
Order CBC/coagulation and cause-directed testing; do not delay stabilization for diagnostic completeness in active major bleeding.
management: Major hemoptysis requires airway protection, acute-care resuscitation and urgent bronchoscopy/interventional radiology/thoracic expertise.
Treat infection, PE, malignancy or other cause once stabilized.
Review/reverse anticoagulation only when clinically indicated and according to drug/severity-specific guidance.
medicationSafety: Anticoagulant interruption/reversal must balance active bleeding against thrombosis risk and use drug-specific pathways.
Avoid NSAIDs/antiplatelet escalation in unexplained active pulmonary bleeding without a clear indication.
counselling: Any recurrent or increasing hemoptysis needs reassessment even if a prior episode was labelled bronchitis.
Teach urgent return for dyspnea, dizziness, larger-volume bleeding or chest pain.
followUp: Ensure abnormal imaging and malignancy/TB testing are closed-loop.
Persistent unexplained hemoptysis requires specialist evaluation.
examTrap: Reassuring repeated hemoptysis as bronchitis in a high-risk smoker without imaging/workup—or defining danger by one arbitrary volume threshold.
oneLinePearl: Hemoptysis becomes life-threatening when blood threatens the airway or circulation.
sourceBasis: Canadian respiratory and acute-care practice standards
Canadian Tuberculosis Standards where TB is suspected

title: Chronic Cough Diagnostic Algorithm
bottomLine: Chronic cough requires a structured differential before repeated empiric therapies. Check red flags and medication/exposure causes, obtain appropriate chest imaging/spirometry, then target common causes such as upper-airway disease, asthma/eosinophilic airway disease and reflux only when the phenotype supports them.
recognize: Smoking/vaping, ACE inhibitors, asthma, upper-airway cough syndromes, eosinophilic bronchitis and reflux are common contributors.
Cough can be multifactorial and may persist after the original trigger resolves.
differentiate: Hemoptysis, weight loss, fever, hypoxemia, abnormal imaging or progressive dyspnea are not routine chronic-cough phenotypes.
TB, ILD, bronchiectasis and malignancy must be considered when risk or red flags fit.
assessment: Clarify duration, triggers, nocturnal/exertional pattern, sputum, reflux/nasal symptoms, medications, smoking/vaping, occupation, TB/travel and cancer risk.
Assess weight, oxygenation, chest exam and ENT findings.
workup: Use chest radiography and spirometry in persistent cough when indicated; obtain CT or specialty testing for abnormal imaging, red flags or refractory unexplained cough.
Avoid indiscriminate broad testing when a clear common cause is supported.
management: Stop an offending ACE inhibitor when appropriate and allow sufficient washout.
Treat confirmed/suspected asthma/eosinophilic airway disease, upper-airway disease or reflux according to phenotype, with a defined response window.
Refer refractory unexplained cough or concerning structural disease.
medicationSafety: Avoid indefinite empiric PPI, antibiotic or opioid cough-suppressant therapy without reassessing the diagnosis.
Sedating antitussives can impair driving/falls risk.
counselling: Explain that chronic cough often requires sequential testing/treatment trials with clear stop points.
Address smoking/vaping and occupational exposure without blame.
followUp: Document whether each targeted intervention improved cough; lack of response should change the hypothesis rather than trigger indefinite continuation.
examTrap: Prescribing repeated antibiotics or PPIs for chronic cough without checking ACE inhibitors, chest imaging, spirometry and red flags.
oneLinePearl: Chronic cough is a differential diagnosis with response checkpoints, not a refill problem.
sourceBasis: Canadian respiratory primary-care practice principles
Canadian Thoracic Society asthma/COPD/ILD guidance

title: Tuberculosis Screening and Treatment
bottomLine: Separate TB infection from TB disease. TST/IGRA identify infection risk; they do not diagnose active pulmonary TB in adults. Suspected disease requires appropriate imaging and microbiology, airborne precautions/public-health action when indicated, and multi-drug treatment through an experienced TB pathway.
recognize: Chronic cough, fever, night sweats, weight loss, hemoptysis and epidemiologic risk can suggest active TB.
Risk is higher with close exposure, prior residence in higher-incidence regions, immune suppression and selected social/structural vulnerabilities.
differentiate: TB infection is asymptomatic without active disease; active TB can transmit and requires disease treatment/public-health management.
A positive TST/IGRA cannot distinguish active disease from infection and is not recommended to diagnose adult TB disease.
assessment: Assess symptoms, exposure history, prior testing/treatment, country/region history, immune status, pregnancy, HIV risk and medication interactions.
Use culturally safe, non-stigmatizing assessment, including for Indigenous and newcomer patients.
workup: Suspected pulmonary TB requires chest imaging plus appropriate respiratory specimens for smear/culture and NAAT; obtain drug-susceptibility testing on confirmed disease.
Use TST or IGRA for TB infection testing only when testing is indicated and treatment would be offered if positive.
management: Report active TB as required and coordinate with public health/TB expertise.
Most drug-susceptible TB begins with a multi-drug intensive regimen while susceptibility is established, then continues with a validated continuation regimen.
Treat TB infection with current preventive-treatment regimens after active disease has been excluded.
medicationSafety: TB therapy has major hepatic, ocular and drug-interaction considerations; rifamycins cause many clinically significant interactions.
Pregnancy, HIV, renal/liver disease and advanced age require regimen-specific expertise and monitoring.
counselling: Explain infection versus disease, adherence, contact/public-health follow-up and expected monitoring.
Address barriers such as housing, transportation, cost and stigma; Canadian TB programs support treatment access.
followUp: Monitor response, toxicity and adherence through the TB program; follow post-treatment recurrence risk when indicated.
Ensure stable primary-care linkage before treatment completion.
examTrap: Using a positive IGRA to diagnose active TB disease—or using NAAT to monitor treatment response/contagiousness after treatment begins.
oneLinePearl: TST/IGRA detect infection; active TB is a microbiology-and-imaging diagnosis with public-health consequences.
sourceBasis: Canadian Tuberculosis Standards, 8th edition
Public Health Agency of Canada TB resources

title: Bronchiectasis Diagnosis and Management
bottomLine: Bronchiectasis is structural airway dilation with recurrent infection/inflammation. Confirm with CT, identify treatable causes and airway-clearance needs, and use sputum microbiology to guide exacerbation therapy rather than giving repeated empiric antibiotics without a culture strategy.
recognize: Chronic productive cough, recurrent chest infections, hemoptysis and persistent crackles raise suspicion.
Pseudomonas or recurrent unusual organisms increase disease complexity and specialist needs.
differentiate: COPD/asthma can coexist but do not explain recurrent purulent sputum/CT bronchial dilation alone.
Cystic fibrosis, immune deficiency, ABPA, aspiration and ciliary disease are important etiologic considerations.
assessment: Assess sputum burden, exacerbation frequency, hemoptysis, weight, sinus disease, aspiration, childhood infection history and immune/autoimmune clues.
Review prior sputum cultures and antibiotic exposure.
workup: Confirm with high-resolution chest CT and obtain sputum cultures, including targeted testing for atypical pathogens when indicated.
Use cause-directed immune, CF, ABPA or aspiration evaluation based on phenotype.
management: Teach regular airway-clearance techniques and physical activity; refer to respiratory physiotherapy when available.
Treat exacerbations using prior/current sputum microbiology and local susceptibility patterns.
Specialist care is indicated for frequent exacerbations, Pseudomonas, significant hemoptysis or advanced disease.
medicationSafety: Repeated broad antibiotics increase resistance and C. difficile risk; culture-directed therapy is preferred.
Long-term macrolide therapy requires specialist-style selection and QT/hearing/mycobacterial considerations.
redFlags: Weight loss or progressive lung-function decline
counselling: Teach airway clearance, hydration/activity, vaccination and when sputum change warrants culture/assessment.
Explain that the goal is preventing exacerbations and preserving lung function, not simply suppressing cough.
followUp: Track exacerbations, sputum microbiology, symptoms, weight and lung function.
Reassess etiology if the course is atypical or rapidly progressive.
examTrap: Treating every flare with the same empiric antibiotic without checking prior sputum microbiology or airway-clearance adherence.
oneLinePearl: Bronchiectasis care is airway clearance plus microbiology plus cause-finding.
sourceBasis: Canadian respiratory bronchiectasis practice principles
Canadian Thoracic Society respiratory infection/airway disease resources

title: Pulmonary Function Test Interpretation
bottomLine: Interpret PFTs in sequence: test quality, obstruction, bronchodilator response, restriction, diffusion and clinical context. A spirometric pattern is not a diagnosis, and race-based assumptions should not substitute for appropriate reference equations and clinical interpretation.
recognize: Reduced FEV1/FVC below the appropriate lower limit supports obstruction.
Low FVC with preserved ratio can suggest restriction but requires lung-volume confirmation.
Reduced DLCO can reflect emphysema, ILD, pulmonary vascular disease, anemia and other causes.
differentiate: Obstruction, restriction and mixed defects are physiologic patterns rather than disease names.
Poor effort, early termination or leak can create misleading abnormalities; always assess test quality.
assessment: Know the clinical question, smoking/exposure history, symptoms, medications and recent bronchodilator use.
Consider hemoglobin and comorbid disease when interpreting DLCO.
workup: Use spirometry, bronchodilator testing, lung volumes and diffusion capacity according to the diagnostic question.
Compare with prior tests when assessing progression, but account for equipment/reference differences.
management: Use the physiologic pattern to refine the differential and choose next tests/therapy.
Refer unexplained restriction, severe diffusion impairment, discordant symptoms or complex mixed disease.
medicationSafety: Do not escalate inhaled therapy solely because FEV1 is low without confirming the disease phenotype and symptoms/exacerbations.
Withhold/continue bronchodilators before testing only according to the lab’s diagnostic protocol.
redFlags: Test pattern inconsistent with the presumed diagnosis
counselling: Explain that PFTs measure physiology and must be interpreted with symptoms and imaging.
Teach why repeated testing may be needed to document progression or treatment response.
followUp: Repeat PFTs when the result will answer a longitudinal clinical question, not by automatic schedule alone.
examTrap: Calling low FVC 'restriction' without lung volumes or calling every obstructive pattern COPD.
oneLinePearl: PFTs describe physiology; the clinician supplies the diagnosis.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society pulmonary function testing guidance
CTS 2023 position on race and ethnicity in PFT interpretation

title: Oxygen Therapy Indications and Prescribing
bottomLine: Oxygen is a drug with an indication and target. Treat hypoxemia, not breathlessness alone; prescribe a target saturation appropriate to the clinical syndrome and recognize patients at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure who require controlled oxygen and ventilatory assessment.
recognize: Hypoxemia can occur with pneumonia, COPD exacerbation, PE, pulmonary edema, ILD and other cardiopulmonary emergencies.
Some chronic respiratory patients can retain CO2 and deteriorate with uncontrolled oxygen; oxygen does not directly correct hypoventilation.
differentiate: Dyspnea with normal oxygenation does not automatically require oxygen.
Long-term oxygen therapy has evidence-based eligibility criteria and is different from short-term oxygen for an acute illness.
assessment: Assess SpO2 quality, respiratory rate/work, mental status, perfusion and risk of chronic hypercapnia.
When hypercapnia is plausible, obtain blood gas assessment and evaluate need for non-invasive ventilation.
workup: Use arterial/venous blood gas and imaging/labs according to the underlying cause.
For home oxygen, confirm eligibility under current provincial/territorial/respiratory program criteria rather than prescribing from one transient low reading.
management: Prescribe oxygen with a documented target and delivery device, then titrate/reassess.
Use controlled oxygen in patients at risk for hypercapnic respiratory failure while addressing the cause and considering non-invasive ventilation.
Long-term/home oxygen should be reassessed after recovery when prescribed during an acute episode.
medicationSafety: Excess oxygen can worsen hypercapnia in susceptible patients; inadequate oxygen is also harmful—use a target rather than reflex restriction.
Fire risk is substantial with smoking/open flame around home oxygen.
counselling: Teach device use, prescribed target/flow instructions and fire safety.
Explain that oxygen treats low oxygen levels; it is not a general treatment for breathlessness.
followUp: Reassess oxygen requirement after treatment of the acute cause and periodically for long-term therapy.
Escalate worsening gas exchange rather than simply increasing flow indefinitely.
examTrap: Giving high-flow oxygen automatically for every dyspneic COPD patient without a target or checking for hypercapnia.
oneLinePearl: Oxygen needs a target, a cause and reassessment.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society COPD/home ventilation guidance
Canadian acute respiratory care practice standards

title: Lung Cancer Screening Criteria and Follow-Up
bottomLine: Lung-cancer screening is for asymptomatic high-risk people and uses low-dose CT, not chest x-ray. Eligibility and implementation vary by province/program; symptoms such as hemoptysis or persistent concerning cough require a diagnostic pathway instead of a screening pathway.
recognize: Smoking history is the dominant eligibility driver in current Canadian screening programs/recommendations.
Screening has benefits but also false positives, incidental findings, radiation exposure and overdiagnosis.
differentiate: Screening is not diagnostic testing for a symptomatic patient.
Chest x-ray and sputum cytology are not recommended screening substitutes for LDCT.
assessment: Clarify current/former smoking exposure, age, comorbidity, prior cancer, symptoms and ability/willingness to undergo follow-up/treatment.
Use non-stigmatizing smoking assessment and cessation support.
workup: Use the current provincial/territorial organized screening eligibility pathway or validated risk model where applicable.
Symptomatic patients need diagnostic chest imaging and referral based on symptoms/risk, not screening enrollment alone.
management: Refer eligible asymptomatic patients for LDCT screening through the available program/pathway.
Ensure abnormal screens enter the program’s nodule follow-up/diagnostic algorithm.
Offer evidence-based smoking cessation support regardless of screening decision.
medicationSafety: No medication substitutes for appropriate screening or smoking cessation support.
Avoid unnecessary antibiotics for abnormal imaging without an infectious syndrome.
counselling: Explain benefits/limitations, possible false positives and need for follow-up.
Clarify that a normal screening CT does not make future concerning symptoms safe to ignore.
followUp: Track the next LDCT or diagnostic step and ensure responsibility is explicit.
Reassess eligibility as age, smoking history, health and provincial programs change.
examTrap: Ordering a screening LDCT for a patient with hemoptysis instead of switching to diagnostic evaluation—or using chest x-ray as the screening test.
oneLinePearl: Asymptomatic high risk = screening; symptoms = diagnosis.
sourceBasis: Canadian Cancer Society lung cancer screening guidance reviewed 2025-2026
